topic: Pizza Bot: an inbox for background AI agents — the new async agent pattern
keyword: pizza bot inbox background ai agents
summary: Pizza Bot (pizza-bot-app/pizza-bot) is an Apache-2.0, self-hosted 'inbox' for AI agents that run in the background: finished work lands in Unread, work that needs a human decision lands in Action, and the runtime checkpoints every step with DeepAgents + LangGraph so an approval pause survives closing the thread, the browser tab, or the app. It was announced by two AWS staffers on 2026-09-10 as an AWS open-source blog post, but it is NOT an AWS service: it lives in its own GitHub org, ships no support or SLA, and the Amazon-specific skills/MCP catalog that made the internal version useful did not come out with it. Verified directly via the GitHub API on 2026-09-29: 402 stars, 35 forks, 18 open issues, 106 commits, 7 contributors, repo created 2026-06-26, last push 2026-09-26, two releases (v1.0.0 on 2026-09-08, v1.1.0 on 2026-09-19) totaling 433 asset downloads. The pattern is not new — LangChain introduced 'ambient agents' in January 2025 and shipped an Agent Inbox (now archived, 1,093 stars); Cloudflare shipped agentic-inbox (8,127 stars) in April 2026. What is new is that a hyperscaler-adjacent team productized it as a finished, non-technical-user application, and that the honest caveats (approval fatigue, no SLA, unbounded checkpoint DB, thin skill catalog) are documented in public issues.
verdict_headline: The inbox idea is right and the durability engineering is real, but Pizza Bot's novelty is overstated, its public version ships thinner than the internal one, and the pattern's failure mode — approval fatigue — is one the inbox itself can amplify.

app.name: Pizza Bot
app.org: pizza-bot-app (standalone GitHub org, separate from Amazon/AWS)
app.description: A local-first inbox for long-running AI agents, built with DeepAgents and LangGraph
app.platforms: Electron desktop (macOS/Windows/Linux) + browser client + terminal CLI, all HTTP/SSE clients of one api-server
app.telemetry: none; api-server binds 127.0.0.1 by default and non-loopback binding requires auth + explicit origin allowlist

runtime.checkpoint_store: SQLite (threads, checkpoints, memories, attachments, logs as files)

competitors.title: AWS open-sources Pizza Bot: email-style inbox for background AI agents (The New Stack, 2026-09-10, Paul Sawers)
key_points: Breaking-news framing: chat is a poor fit for agents whose work continues after the user logs off, so Pizza Bot borrows email mechanics — completed jobs as unread threads, decisions surfaced for action

Reports the lineage claim that weakens novelty: LangChain CEO Harrison Chase introduced 'ambient agents' in January 2025 with an email-assistant reference implementation on LangGraph, plus a standalone 'Agent Inbox' interface

Quotes co-creator Joseph Dolivo (principal technologist, AWS Startups) on the goal: 'scheduled agents run autonomously in the background and surface updates directly into your inbox for review and triage'
Traces the origin story: April 2025 'JoeBot' side project that automated CRM logging, then an internal MCP server with deterministic 'recipes', then the rebuild as an Electron desktop app
Documents the key pivot: 'an MCP server requires an MCP client, and expecting non-technical users to work out of an IDE or terminal was never going to cut it'
Notes that despite Amazon roots it is a standalone community project with no AWS support or SLA, fully self-hosted, storing threads and checkpoints in local SQLite and ordinary files
Confirms the bundled browser-automation skill uses Playwright MCP — so 'local-first' does not mean 'no network access'

competitors.title: Introducing Pizza Bot, an open source inbox for AI agents that work in the background (AWS Open Source Blog, 2026-09-10)
key_points: Primary source for the design brief: 'The interface assumes you are not watching. Nothing else we've seen starts there, and that one assumption is what buys you pauses that outlast the session that created them'

Justifies the email metaphor directly: 'You don't send an email and then sit watching the outbox until the reply lands' and 'a thread is a unit of work you come back to rather than a session you have to attend'

Defines the three queues: All (thread history), Unread (completed work not yet reviewed), Action (paused, waiting on approval or an answer), plus an Activity panel showing delegated specialists' own transcripts
Four recurring requirements from internal workflows: inspect several sources, prepare a result in the background, ask before consequential action, come find the person who asked when done

Architecture: server runs the agent and owns state; clients are Electron, browser, or terminal; a run keeps going when you close the thread or switch devices; put the server on an always-on machine or container to keep schedules firing
Extension model uses existing conventions rather than bespoke ones: SKILL.md skills, MCP servers, plugins, and a Claude Code-compatible .mcp.json that drops straight in

Explicit no-support disclaimer: 'Pizza Bot is a community project rather than an AWS service, so there's no AWS support or service-level agreement behind it; keeping Pizza Bot running, backed up, and up to date is yours'

Cron catch-up semantics worth quoting: after downtime the scheduler runs a slept-through occurrence once rather than replaying every missed interval — 'a machine that spent a month switched off gives you one result instead of thirty'
Roadmap is stated as principles, not dates: own your data, bring your own model (including local), build what's missing

competitors.title: AWS bets that AI agents need an inbox, not another chat window (Computerworld/InfoWorld, 2026-09-16, Anirban Ghoshal)
key_points: The only coverage in this set with substantive analyst pushback — the strongest source for a critical section

Kanerika CRO Bhupendra Chopra: 'Integration is where most of the money in an enterprise agent deployment goes' — out-of-the-box skills save app-building time but not the CRM/email/ERP connector work someone must build, secure and maintain
Nord-IQ analyst Manoj Chandra Jha: lack of support or SLA pushes the integration and operational burden onto the enterprise

HFS Research CEO Phil Fersht on the core structural risk: 'The inbox model can make bad work less visible. When somebody is watching an agent in a chat window, they can see it going off the rails' — with hundreds of background tasks, problems surface only at completion
Chopra names approval fatigue explicitly: 'An agent sending back dozens of threads with multiple approval requests can condition users to approve them without reading them closely'
Staleness risk: information current when the agent paused may be invalid hours later when the human approves

Positive case is framed as economics, not UX: a chat interface requires attention throughout, an inbox brings the human in only when judgment is needed; the analogy is coding agents where an engineer assigns an issue and reviews the PR
Notes the stack explicitly: DeepAgents as harness, LangGraph as stateful runtime, Hono server between runtime and UI/skills/MCP/provider

competitors.title: AWS Introduces Pizza Bot: An Open Source Inbox for Background AI Agents (MarkTechPost, 2026-09-13)
key_points: Best single source for the mechanical caveats a review must state precisely

Internal scale datapoint: earlier versions 'served more than 2,000 people inside Amazon' for meeting prep, email drafting, Slack summaries, CRM logging and research — this describes the predecessor MCP server, not the released app

Quitting the desktop app stops its embedded server and ends active runs; checkpoints preserve the thread but the step in flight can be lost — an always-on backend is required for work to continue after the desktop exits
Two separate SQLite stores: LangGraph checkpoints for thread state, plus separate stores for cross-thread memory and app metadata

Skill approval policy is declarative per tool: interruptOn decides which tool calls stop for a human, allowedDecisions decides which buttons appear; users can approve, edit proposed arguments, or reject
A skill only becomes callable once the servers and tools it declares are actually available, and the Skills screen shows which ones are not
Safety envelope of the built-in interpreter is narrow: sandboxed JavaScript with no network and no host filesystem access, plus explicit per-folder filesystem grants

competitors.title: AWS Open-Sources Pizza Bot, an Inbox for Background AI Agents (Techstrong.ai, 2026-09-11, Steven Vaughan-Nichols)
key_points: Leads with the governance fact most reviews bury: 'AWS's Pizza Bot is not an AWS-supported service. You're on your own'

Quotes the load-bearing rationale sentence: 'Live chat assumes both parties are present. That holds for a quick exchange and breaks the moment a task takes several minutes, waits on your approval, or runs on a schedule while you're away'
Notes triggers: manual start, webhook, or cron — scheduled work and typed work share the same persistence, approvals, notifications and inbox downstream

Frames the usefulness risk correctly: 'The project's usefulness will depend heavily on the open-source community building integrations to replace the Amazon-specific skills and MCP connections excluded from the public version'
Confirms state location: threads, checkpoints, memories, attachments, configuration and logs stored in a local folder as SQLite databases and plain files

competitors.title: Show HN: Pizza Bot – An inbox for AI agents that work in the background (2026-09-15, 61 points, 37 comments)
key_points: The creator's own AMA is the best source for honest limits — several answers retract implied capability

Sandboxing is deferred: Pizza Bot ships a QuickJS interpreter but 'otherwise, sandboxing is something we deferred until after launch' — LangGraph/DeepAgents hooks are cited as the future path, not a shipped feature
Structured/constrained output does not work as asked: a user wanting enforced JSON/XML via task({responseSchema}) got 'this doesn't work out of the box', and the creator filed issue #98 to enable it

Positioning vs. Paperclip, in the creator's words: Paperclip 'provides orchestration over a fleet of existing agent harnesses, whereas with Pizza Bot, we run the execution loops for each agent ourselves' and Pizza Bot sticks to a thread model rather than a task model

Positioning vs. ticket trackers (Linear): you'd still connect Linear's MCP server for 'what needs doing'; Pizza Bot owns the run, approvals routing and state — the differentiator claimed is N agents in one inbox instead of N terminal tabs

'Why not real email?' answered as a deliberate choice: borrow the UX, not the implementation, so there is no email dependency and the app can run fully offline with local models (AgentMail-style per-agent addresses are acknowledged as a separate approach)
Desktop-only objection corrected in public: it is both — the creator runs the backend in Docker on a home network and reaches it from a phone over Tailscale

Real onboarding friction reported by a user running local models through llama.cpp: model list refresh bugs and a 'New Chat' showing one model while hitting the provider with another; judged 'a bit rough' but 'easy and clean' overall

A creator response concedes documentation is missing an architecture diagram for the orchestrator-subagent/Skill mapping, and that per-skill subagent model override is not yet shipped (issues #99, #100 filed during the thread)

competitors.title: Your AI agents' reports and questions have a new inbox, courtesy of AWS (The Register, 2026-09-15)
key_points: Condenses the metaphor into a quotable line: like an email client because 'a thread is a unit of work you come back to rather than a session you have to attend'
Maps the queues to work types: finished tasks with detailed result writeups land in Unread; anything requiring a decision is shunted to Action
Frames the value for people juggling multiple 'digital delegees' rather than for builders — the non-developer audience is the differentiator against terminal/IDE-shaped agent tooling
Groups Pizza Bot with hosted assistants as a contrast: self-hosted means you own the model and the data boundary, versus an assistant running on somebody else's infrastructure

competitors.title: Background agents need an inbox, not chat windows (OOMeta AI, September 2026)
key_points: Treats the release as evidence for a general supervision pattern rather than a product review: 'asynchronous agents need an asynchronous supervision surface'
Extracts three transferable design rules: separate finished output from pending decisions; make approval editable rather than reject-and-rerun; don't outsource supervision data

Distinguishes output shape from logging: each background agent should produce 'a letter, not a log' with what it did, where the evidence is, and who must decide what — if you can't name the decider, the task isn't decomposed to a supervisable granularity
Recommends writing approval policy per tool rather than handing the agent an all-access key — the interruptOn pattern, generalized
Argues the value of edit-as-a-decision is reducing the cost of human correction, because reject-and-rerun-only surfaces push supervisors toward 'fine, leave it'

competitors.title: LangGraph / DeepAgents runtime context — the mechanism behind durable pauses
key_points: Pizza Bot's durability is not custom: LangGraph persists a checkpoint at each graph step, and an interrupt stops the graph at a declared point so the run resumes from the record rather than from scratch
This is exactly why an approval can outlive the session that created it — the pause is disk state, not a held connection
DeepAgents supplies the harness layer on top (task delegation, subagents, filesystem tooling), which Pizza Bot maps 1:1 to Skills

Consequence for reviewers: 'pauses that outlast the session' is an engineering property you can inspect, not a marketing claim — the same property LangChain demonstrated in January 2025's ambient-agent email assistant

competitors.title: langchain-ai/agent-inbox — the archived predecessor (1,093 stars, MIT, created 2024-11-04, archived)
key_points: Direct evidence against 'nothing else starts there': a standalone agent-inbox UX for human-in-the-loop agents existed almost two years earlier and is now archived
Scoped differently though — it required a running LangGraph deployment and a LangGraph API key, i.e. infrastructure-first, not a finished desktop application
That scope difference is Pizza Bot's real contribution: packaged app + local runtime + skills/MCP catalog for people who will never open a terminal
Useful contrast metric: 1,093 stars on a developer-only tool that went archived vs 402 stars on the packaged app within ~3 months of public creation

competitors.title: cloudflare/agentic-inbox — the concurrent alternative (8,127 stars, Apache-2.0, created 2026-04-10)
key_points: A second independent project landed on the inbox metaphor within months of Pizza Bot, which supports 'the pattern is converging' over 'AWS invented it'
Inverts the deployment axis: a self-hosted email client with an AI agent running entirely on Cloudflare Workers — cloud infrastructure rather than local-first storage
Different trust model: the agent reads your real inbox and drafts replies you approve before they send, so the human-in-the-loop gate is on outbound communication
Useful for a comparison section: local-first/Ollama-capable (Pizza Bot) vs serverless/Cloudflare-hosted (agentic-inbox) — same UX thesis, opposite data-residency answers

stats.fact: Stack Overflow pulse survey (1,100 respondents, April 2026): agent use at work jumped to 59% from 31%, but 63% of technologists still rarely or never let agents run fully on autopilot and 60% block agents from making unapproved system changes
Same survey: 69% run a single agent, 17% multiple specialized agents, 16% multiple overlapping/coordinated agents — multi-agent supervision surfaces serve a minority today

Amazon Security VP Eric Brandwine (2026-06-21): 'Human-in-the-loop isn't necessarily the gold standard' — reviewers do a good job, then an okay job, then pretty quickly a poor job

Gartner Q1 2026 with S&P Global: 80% of enterprise applications shipped or updated embed at least one AI agent, but only 31% of organizations have one in production; 88% of agent pilots never reach production
Cloudflare's agentic-inbox reached 8,127 stars (Apache-2.0, created 2026-04-10, last push 2026-04-23), showing the inbox pattern independently attracted far more attention than Pizza Bot's 402
LangChain's Agent Inbox — a direct predecessor — has 1,093 stars, was created 2024-11-04, was last pushed 2026-09-18, and is now archived

angles: The inbox is a supervision pattern, not a chat replacement: separate 'finished work' (Unread) from 'needs your decision' (Action) so a returning human triages by priority instead of scrolling logs — that split, not the email skin, is the transferable idea

'Nothing else we've seen starts there' is the weakest claim in the launch: LangChain named ambient agents in January 2025 and shipped an Agent Inbox (now archived, 1,093 stars), and Cloudflare shipped agentic-inbox (8,127 stars) five months before Pizza Bot — the pattern was already converging

What Pizza Bot actually contributes is packaging and audience, not invention: a finished Electron app plus local runtime plus skills/MCP catalog aimed at people who will never open a terminal, against Agent Inbox's requirement of a running LangGraph deployment and API key

Durable pauses are the real engineering story: LangGraph checkpoints to SQLite, so an approval can outlive the session that created it — 'the interface assumes you are not watching' is an architectural property you can inspect, not a slogan

Approval fatigue is the pattern's built-in failure mode and Pizza Bot can amplify it: dozens of threads each carrying approval requests condition users to approve without reading, and one-third of malicious coding-agent commands were approved in a controlled simulation

Counter-intuitive finding worth leading with in a critical section: safety is an inverted-U in escalation rate — escalating every risky action to a degrading human can be less safe than escalating fewer, which argues interruptOn should be narrow by tool, not broad

The inbox hides failure as well as it hides noise: watching an agent in a chat window reveals it going off the rails, but hundreds of quiet background threads surface mistakes only at completion (Fersht) — and a paused approval can be stale by the time a human sees it

Integration, not UI, is where the money goes: Pizza Bot ships the app and leaves the CRM/email/ERP connectors to you, with no SLA behind the result (Chopra, Jha) — the honest enterprise verdict is 'the demo is easy, the deployment is not'

Local-first as a trust architecture rather than a performance claim: no telemetry, 127.0.0.1 by default, auth plus origin allowlist for non-loopback, secrets in the OS keychain, per-folder explicit grants, and a model list that includes Ollama so the data need never leave — directly contrasted with Cloudflare's serverless agentic-inbox

Adoption is far behind attention: 402 stars and 433 release downloads across two releases, i.e. the launch generated coverage, not installs — a good reality anchor for any 'agents are taking over' narrative

The internal-vs-public gap is the product's central problem: 2,000 Amazon users relied on an internal skill/MCP catalog that could not be open-sourced, so the released app ships thinner while the community is asked to rebuild the catalog — 'usefulness depends on the community' (Techstrong)

Read the open issues as the honest changelog: unbounded checkpoint growth (1.24 GB for 32 threads, #58), structured output unsupported (#98), no per-skill model override (#99), MCP servers inert until a skill declares their tools (#100), approvals showing what an agent wants to do but not why it believes it (#111)

Caveat users will hit on day one: quitting the desktop app kills its embedded server and the in-flight step, even though the checkpointed thread survives — the always-on backend or container is the actually-supported deployment for unattended work

faq.q: Is Pizza Bot an AWS product?
faq.a: No. It was announced on the AWS Open Source Blog by two AWS staffers on 2026-09-10, but it lives in its own GitHub org with no AWS support and no SLA, and it is Apache-2.0 and fully self-hosted. Keeping it running, backed up and updated is the operator's job.

faq.q: What does the inbox actually change compared to a chat window?
faq.a: It separates two things chat conflates: work that finished (Unread) and work waiting on a human decision (Action). A returning operator triages a queue instead of watching a stream. The Activity panel additionally shows delegated specialist subagents and their tool calls in-place.

faq.q: How do approvals survive if I close the app?
faq.a: DeepAgents/LangGraph checkpoints the run to a local SQLite database at each step, and an approved pause resumes from that checkpoint rather than restarting. Quitting the desktop app stops its embedded server and can lose the step in flight, so unattended work needs the backend on an always-on machine or in a container.

faq.q: Is the 'inbox for agents' idea new with Pizza Bot?
faq.a: No. LangChain introduced 'ambient agents' in January 2025 with an email-assistant reference implementation and shipped a standalone Agent Inbox (now archived, 1,093 stars). Cloudflare's agentic-inbox (8,127 stars) shipped in April 2026. Pizza Bot's contribution is packaging the pattern as a finished, non-technical-user application.

faq.q: What are the real risks of the pattern?
faq.a: Approval fatigue (people approve without reading — about one-third of malicious coding-agent commands were approved in a controlled simulation), reduced visibility of failure while many tasks run quietly, and stale approvals when information changes between pause and decision.

faq.q: Which model providers are supported, and can it run fully offline?
faq.a: Amazon Bedrock, Anthropic, Google Gemini, OpenAI, OpenRouter, and Ollama. With a local model serving through Ollama, self-hosted storage, no telemetry, and default loopback-only binding, nothing has to leave the machine.

faq.q: What does the public version lack compared to the internal one?
faq.a: The internal catalog of skills and MCP servers for Amazon's own systems could not be released, so the app ships thinner than the version 2,000+ Amazon users relied on, and community-built integrations are where its usefulness now depends.
